the industrialization of American astronomy occurred between 1880 and 1940.

the development of big American astronomy was the result of the interaction of four forces: the rise of the American industrial system; the emergence of the professional research university; the rise of a professional scientific community; and the growth of a national scientific bureaucracy.

the industrialization of American astronomy, the development of big astronomy, and the emergence of astronomy as the biggest of sciences in an age when science was still little science, occurred in the six decades before 1940.

the following questions: What were the social, cultural, and economic factors that led to the industrialization of American astronomy? the development of astronomy as a science was a process that took place in the United States in the 19th and 20th centuries.
the Industrial Revolution and the Industrialization of Astronomy were the two main reasons for the rise of Big Science.

“Big science is the result of the interaction between the scientific community and society, in which the latter provides the resources for the former to pursue its goals.” This statement is a general one, but it can be applied to specific cases, such as the development of nuclear physics in the United States in the 1930s, the Manhattan Project, and the development of the hydrogen bomb.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the industrialization of American astronomy was the product of the confluence of three factors: (1) the rise of professional astronomy in the United States; (2) the rise of the American astronomical observatory; and (3) the rise of industrial astronomy in America.
, in the United States, astronomy became a big science before physics.

the industrialization of American astronomy was driven by the needs of the American astronomical community to solve problems that required large-scale data collection, data analysis, and the construction of large instruments, and that the industrialization was made possible by the emergence of a new class of professional astronomers who were able to communicate with and manage industrial organizations.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the development of big astronomy in America was not simply a matter of government support, but was also a matter of the changing nature of the scientific enterprise and the emergence of a new class of scientists who were able to take advantage of the new opportunities for big science.
astronomy's rise to prominence was a product of the industrialization of science, which was a process of the transformation of science into a large-scale, bureaucratic, corporate enterprise.
the rise of big science was not a response to the exigencies of war, but rather a response to the needs of a new economy.
